What drives Olist delivery times, and what logistics and operations teams should do about it

The answer in one paragraph

Delivery time on Olist is driven mainly by route: where the seller is, where the customer is, and whether the two are in the same state. Product and order characteristics add a smaller amount, and purchase timing adds less than route, although the slow months matter: in the scenarios below, a November order takes several days longer than an August order on the same route. The best model (Decision Tree on R3 + Olist estimate) predicts delivery time on unseen orders to within about 4.8 days on average and explains about 31% of the variation, using only information available at or shortly after checkout. That is 24% lower error than always predicting the average (6.3 days), and 9% lower than the first-draft model (5.2 days), which used fewer features (it was refit on the same order-grouped split, so the comparison is fair). Olist’s own checkout estimate is much looser: on its own it explains only 15% of the variation, and on the test orders it is on average 11.5 days longer than what actually happened. What follows turns those findings into concrete order scenarios and recommendations.

How delivery time varies by route

We group test orders into route tiers: orders where seller and customer are in the same state, and cross-state orders by the customer’s macro-region. The table compares what customers were promised, what actually happened, and how well the model did.

Code 
# Brazil's five macro-regions, used to group destination states into service tiers
macro_region <- function(state) {
  case_when(
    state %in% c("AC", "AM", "AP", "PA", "RO", "RR", "TO") ~ "North",
    state %in% c("AL", "BA", "CE", "MA", "PB", "PE", "PI", "RN", "SE") ~ "Northeast",
    state %in% c("DF", "GO", "MS", "MT") ~ "Center-West",
    state %in% c("ES", "MG", "RJ", "SP") ~ "Southeast",
    state %in% c("PR", "RS", "SC") ~ "South",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )
}

tier_levels <- c("Same state", "Cross-state to Southeast", "Cross-state to South",
                 "Cross-state to Center-West", "Cross-state to Northeast",
                 "Cross-state to North")

tp <- test_preds |>
  mutate(
    route_tier = if_else(
      same_state == "same", "Same state",
      paste0("Cross-state to ", macro_region(as.character(customer_state)))
    ),
    route_tier = factor(route_tier, levels = tier_levels)
  )

# For each tier: promise vs. actual, plus the 10th and 90th percentile of the residual
# (actual minus predicted), which bound the middle 80% of outcomes around a prediction
tier_tbl <- tp |>
  group_by(route_tier) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    actual = mean(delivery_days),
    olist = mean(estimated_days),
    padding = mean(estimated_days - delivery_days),
    olist_late = mean(delivery_days > estimated_days),
    mae = mean(abs(residual)),
    q10 = quantile(residual, 0.1, names = FALSE),
    q90 = quantile(residual, 0.9, names = FALSE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

tier_tbl |>
  transmute(
    `Route tier` = as.character(route_tier),
    `Test rows` = format(n, big.mark = ","),
    `Avg actual days` = round(actual, 1),
    `Avg Olist estimate` = round(olist, 1),
    `Avg padding (estimate - actual)` = round(padding, 1),
    `Late vs. Olist estimate` = scales::percent(olist_late, accuracy = 0.1),
    `Model MAE (days)` = round(mae, 1),
    `80% window around prediction (days)` = sprintf("%+.0f to %+.0f", q10, q90)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Delivery performance by route tier (test set, decision tree on Recipe 3)")

Code 
tier_tbl |>
  select(route_tier, Actual = actual, `Olist estimate` = olist) |>
  pivot_longer(-route_tier, names_to = "measure", values_to = "days") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = days, y = fct_rev(route_tier), fill = measure)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Actual" = "#2b8cbe", "Olist estimate" = "#d95f02")) +
  labs(
    title = "Olist's estimate is padded on every route, and the padding differs by route",
    x = "Average days", y = NULL, fill = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

What this shows

  • Route is the biggest divide. Average delivery time ranges from 7.3 days (Same state) to 22.3 days (Cross-state to North), a gap of about 3 times.
  • The padding is uneven. Olist’s estimate is longer than actual delivery by 9.9 days on the tier with the least padding (Same state) and 16 days on the tier with the most (Cross-state to North). Overall, 91% of test orders arrive before the estimated date and 7.4% arrive after it.
  • The model is least certain where routes are long. Its average error is 3.3 days on the most predictable tier and 8 days on Cross-state to North. The 80% window (the range that contains the middle 80% of outcomes around the prediction) is about 10 days wide on the narrowest tier and 23 days wide on Cross-state to North.

Six order scenarios, predicted

To make the model concrete, we score six “typical order” profiles. For each one we take real training orders on that route (seller state to customer state), use their median freight, weight, price, size, and Olist estimate, and set the purchase month. August is a fast month in the exploration, and November is a slow one. Both the lasso (the interpretable linear model) and the decision tree (the most accurate model) score each profile.

Code 
# Most common category among a route's orders
mode_level <- function(x) {
  tab <- table(as.character(x))
  x[which(as.character(x) == names(which.max(tab)))[1]]
}

# A "typical order" on a route: median values for numeric fields and the most common
# category for the rest, taken from real training orders, with the purchase month set explicitly
build_scenario <- function(label, seller, cust, month) {
  rows <- train |> filter(seller_state == seller, customer_state == cust)
  stopifnot(nrow(rows) > 0)

  rows |>
    summarise(
      across(where(is.numeric), \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      across(where(is.factor), mode_level)
    ) |>
    select(-delivery_days) |>
    mutate(
      order_id = "scenario",
      purchase_month = factor(as.character(month), levels = levels(train$purchase_month)),
      label = label,
      n_similar = nrow(rows),
      route_median_days = median(rows$delivery_days)
    )
}

scenario_def <- tribble(
  ~label,                                   ~seller, ~cust, ~month,
  "Same state (SP to SP), off-peak (Aug)",  "SP",    "SP",  8,
  "Same state (SP to SP), peak (Nov)",      "SP",    "SP",  11,
  "Neighbouring state (SP to RJ), Aug",     "SP",    "RJ",  8,
  "Northeast (SP to BA), off-peak (Aug)",   "SP",    "BA",  8,
  "Northeast (SP to BA), peak (Nov)",       "SP",    "BA",  11,
  "Remote north (SP to AM), off-peak (Aug)", "SP",   "AM",  8
)

scn_df <- pmap(scenario_def, build_scenario) |> list_rbind()

scn_res <- scn_df |>
  mutate(
    lasso_pred = predict(fit_lasso3, new_data = scn_df)$.pred,
    tree_pred  = predict(fit_tree3,  new_data = scn_df)$.pred,
    olist_estimate = estimated_days
  ) |>
  select(label, n_similar, route_median_days, olist_estimate, lasso_pred, tree_pred)

scn_res |>
  transmute(
    Scenario = label,
    `Similar training orders` = format(n_similar, big.mark = ","),
    `Route median, all months (days)` = round(route_median_days, 1),
    `Olist estimate (days)` = round(olist_estimate, 1),
    `Lasso prediction (days)` = round(lasso_pred, 1),
    `Tree prediction (days)` = round(tree_pred, 1)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Predicted delivery days for six typical order profiles")

Code 
scn_res |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, tree_pred)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = label)) +
  geom_col(aes(x = tree_pred), fill = "#2b8cbe", width = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = olist_estimate), shape = 18, size = 4, color = "#d95f02") +
  labs(
    title = "Same seller, different routes: predicted delivery time",
    subtitle = "Bars: decision tree prediction. Diamonds: Olist's estimate for the same profile",
    x = "Days", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

What the scenarios show

  • Route changes the answer more than anything else. Predicted delivery runs from 6.4 days (Same state (SP to SP), off-peak (Aug)) to 17.7 days (Northeast (SP to BA), peak (Nov)) according to the tree.
  • The peak month adds days on the same route. Moving the same-state order from August to November changes the tree prediction by +4.1 days (lasso: +4.9), and moving the Bahia order by +5.8 days (lasso: +4.9). The size of the seasonal effect depends on the route, which only the tree can express fully.
  • The two models agree on the direction, not always on the size. They differ by up to 6.1 days across the six profiles. Where they disagree most, treat the prediction as less certain. The remote-north profile also rests on few similar orders, so read it as an illustration only.
  • Olist’s estimate also changes with route, but not in step with the model. The estimate minus the tree prediction ranges from 6.6 to 26.9 days across the six profiles, so the amount of padding is not the same for every route.

These profiles use real typical values for each route, and the purchase year is set to the most common year on that route. They illustrate the model; they are not forecasts of any single order.

Late deliveries by purchase month

Code 
month_tbl <- tp |>
  mutate(month_num = as.integer(as.character(purchase_month))) |>
  group_by(month_num) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    actual = mean(delivery_days),
    olist = mean(estimated_days),
    late = mean(delivery_days > estimated_days),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(month = factor(month.abb[month_num], levels = month.abb))

ggplot(month_tbl, aes(x = month, y = late)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2b8cbe", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of orders arriving after Olist's estimate, by purchase month",
    subtitle = "Test set, all years pooled",
    x = NULL, y = "Late vs. estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

The late share is highest for orders placed in Mar, Nov, Feb (15.9%, 13.0%, 12.0%) and lowest in Jun (1.7%). Months pool different years in a dataset that covers 2016 to 2018, so some of this reflects specific events or demand peaks in a single year, not a calendar pattern. Compare this with the average delivery time by purchase month in the Exploration page (Section 4.5).

What the team should do

  1. Make the delivery promise route-aware. Set the checkout estimate from seller state, customer state, and month, instead of one rule for everything. The tier table shows how unevenly the current estimate is padded (9.9 days on Same state, 16 days on Cross-state to North). Same-state routes are the natural first pilot: they are the most predictable tier (average miss of 3.3 days) and today’s estimate there is 17.3 days against 7.3 actual. The buffer should be chosen so the late rate stays at or below today’s 5.1% on that tier. A pilot on a few routes would show how many days could be saved. Measure it by: average promised days and the late rate, by route tier.

  2. Show a delivery window, not a single date. Point predictions are good on average but miss the slow tail, and the width of the uncertainty depends on the route (about 10 days on the tightest tier and 23 days on Cross-state to North, measured as the middle 80% of outcomes). Offering “between day X and day Y” is more honest and matches how the model behaves. Measure it by: the share of orders that land inside the window, which should be close to the 80% it is designed for.

  3. Add a seasonal buffer for the slow months. Orders placed in Mar, Nov, Feb are late most often. Extend the promise or add carrier capacity in those months. Check whether the pattern holds in newer data before committing. Measure it by: the late rate in those months, year over year.

  4. Treat the north and northeast as a separate service tier. Routes into these regions are the slowest and the hardest to predict (the highest-error tier is Cross-state to North, with an average miss of 8 days). Set separate expectations, review carrier performance on these lanes, and consider whether stocking inventory closer to these customers is worth testing. Measure it by: delivery time and prediction error on these lanes, tracked separately.

  5. Test whether sourcing closer to the buyer helps. Same-state routes are the fastest, and the same-state flag is among the most important features in the tree (second only to customer state). That is an association, not proof that moving a seller would change delivery time, because sellers and buyers in the same state may also differ in carrier mix and product type. A small pilot, such as a “ships from your state” badge or search ranking, would show whether the effect is real. Measure it by: conversion and delivery time on the pilot group against a control.

  6. Do not spend effort on purchase weekday or time of day. In the Exploration page, weekday moved average delivery time by under two days and time of day by well under a day, against a gap of about a week between same-state and cross-state routes. Put effort into route, carrier, and seller handling instead.

  7. Look at seller handling time. The shipping deadline the seller was given (ship_window_days) is a predictor in the models, and the Exploration page shows median delivery time differing across shipping-window groups. We cannot tell from this data whether sellers who are given more time actually take more time, so this is a question to investigate with seller-level shipping timestamps.

  8. Keep the model honest over time. Retrain on recent orders at a regular interval, watch average error by route tier, and treat a sustained rise in error as a sign that carrier performance or demand has shifted.

How far to trust it

  • Accuracy is useful, not exact. A typical miss is about 4.8 days, and the average error is much smaller than the error on the worst orders (RMSE 7.6 days). This is good for checkout windows and capacity planning, not for day-exact commitments.
  • The slow tail is still hard. The model under-predicts the slowest orders, because it predicts a typical value for a right-skewed target. That is why we recommend a window with a buffer.
  • A random split tests similar orders, not future ones. The test orders come from the same 2016 to 2018 period as the training orders. The model has not been tested on a new carrier contract, a strike, or a different year.
  • Single test set. Differences of a few hundredths of a day between models are not meaningful.
  • Order-item grain. delivery_days is an order-level duration repeated across the items of an order, so multi-item orders carry slightly more weight in the metrics.
  • Associations, not causes. The importance scores and coefficients show what the models rely on to predict. They do not show what causes a delay, which is why recommendations 5 and 7 are framed as tests.
  • Coarse geography. Zip-code region is only a rough stand-in for distance, and the scenarios use median values for each route.

What would improve it next

  • Real seller-to-customer distance from Olist’s geolocation table, which is the most promising feature not yet used.
  • Stage-level timestamps (approval, handoff to carrier, delivery), so seller handling time and carrier transit time can be modelled separately and each team can see its own share.
  • A time-based test: train on earlier months and test on later ones, which is a stricter check than a random split.
  • Non-linear ensemble models and a log-transformed target. These were outside the scope here and were not tested on the order-grouped split. They might lower typical error, at the cost of being harder to explain.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(glmnet)
library(rpart)
library(knitr)
tidymodels_prefer()

needed <- c("data/delivery_train_v2.rds", "data/final_lasso_r3.rds",
            "data/final_tree_r3.rds", "data/model_results.rds",
            "data/test_preds_tree_r3.rds")
missing_files <- needed[!file.exists(needed)]
if (length(missing_files) > 0) {
  stop("Missing model output files: ", paste(missing_files, collapse = ", "))
}

train      <- read_rds("data/delivery_train_v2.rds")
fit_lasso3 <- read_rds("data/final_lasso_r3.rds")
fit_tree3  <- read_rds("data/final_tree_r3.rds")
results    <- read_rds("data/model_results.rds")
test_preds <- read_rds("data/test_preds_tree_r3.rds")

get_metric <- function(rec, mod, met) {
  results[results$recipe == rec & results$model == mod, ][[met]]
}

best_row <- results |>
  filter(recipe != "Benchmark") |>
  slice_min(mae, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

naive_mae  <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Naive (train mean)", "mae")
naive_rmse <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Naive (train mean)", "rmse")
olist_mae  <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Olist estimate only (LM)", "mae")
olist_r2   <- get_metric("Benchmark", "Olist estimate only (LM)", "rsq_trad")
draft_mae  <- get_metric("Benchmark", "First-draft ridge (original features)", "mae")
draft_r2   <- get_metric("Benchmark", "First-draft ridge (original features)", "rsq_trad")

# Olist's promise is the estimated delivery date shown at checkout. An order is late if it
# arrives after that date. Padding is how many days longer the promise was than the actual delivery
mean_actual <- mean(test_preds$delivery_days)
olist_late  <- mean(test_preds$delivery_days > test_preds$estimated_days)
olist_early <- mean(test_preds$delivery_days < test_preds$estimated_days)
mean_olist_padding <- mean(test_preds$estimated_days - test_preds$delivery_days)
```

## The answer in one paragraph

Delivery time on Olist is driven mainly by **route**: where the seller is, where the customer is, and whether the two are in the same state. Product and order characteristics add a smaller amount, and purchase timing adds less than route, although the slow months matter: in the scenarios below, a November order takes several days longer than an August order on the same route. The best model (`r best_row$model` on `r best_row$recipe`) predicts delivery time on unseen orders to within about **`r round(best_row$mae, 1)` days** on average and explains about **`r round(100 * best_row$rsq_trad)`%** of the variation, using only information available at or shortly after checkout. That is `r round(100 * (1 - best_row$mae / naive_mae))`% lower error than always predicting the average (`r round(naive_mae, 1)` days), and `r round(100 * (1 - best_row$mae / draft_mae))`% lower than the first-draft model (`r round(draft_mae, 1)` days), which used fewer features (it was refit on the same order-grouped split, so the comparison is fair). Olist's own checkout estimate is much looser: on its own it explains only `r round(100 * olist_r2)`% of the variation, and on the test orders it is on average `r round(mean_olist_padding, 1)` days longer than what actually happened. What follows turns those findings into concrete order scenarios and recommendations.

We group test orders into route tiers: orders where seller and customer are in the same state, and cross-state orders by the customer's macro-region. The table compares what customers were promised, what actually happened, and how well the model did.

#| label: tier-values

fast_tier  <- tier_tbl$route_tier[which.min(tier_tbl$actual)]
slow_tier  <- tier_tbl$route_tier[which.max(tier_tbl$actual)]

mae_lo <- min(tier_tbl$mae)

**What this shows**

- **Route is the biggest divide.** Average delivery time ranges from `r round(fast_days, 1)` days (`r fast_tier`) to `r round(slow_days, 1)` days (`r slow_tier`), a gap of about `r round(slow_days / fast_days, 1)` times.
- **The padding is uneven.** Olist's estimate is longer than actual delivery by `r round(pad_lo, 1)` days on the tier with the least padding (`r pad_lo_tier`) and `r round(pad_hi, 1)` days on the tier with the most (`r pad_hi_tier`). Overall, `r scales::percent(olist_early, accuracy = 1)` of test orders arrive before the estimated date and `r scales::percent(olist_late, accuracy = 0.1)` arrive after it.
- **The model is least certain where routes are long.** Its average error is `r round(mae_lo, 1)` days on the most predictable tier and `r round(mae_hi, 1)` days on `r mae_hi_tier`. The 80% window (the range that contains the middle 80% of outcomes around the prediction) is about `r round(narrow_width)` days wide on the narrowest tier and `r round(wide_width)` days wide on `r wide_tier`.

---

## Six order scenarios, predicted

To make the model concrete, we score six "typical order" profiles. For each one we take real training orders on that route (seller state to customer state), use their median freight, weight, price, size, and Olist estimate, and set the purchase month. August is a fast month in the exploration, and November is a slow one. Both the lasso (the interpretable linear model) and the decision tree (the most accurate model) score each profile.

```{r}
#| label: scenarios
# Most common category among a route's orders
mode_level <- function(x) {
  tab <- table(as.character(x))
  x[which(as.character(x) == names(which.max(tab)))[1]]
}

# A "typical order" on a route: median values for numeric fields and the most common
# category for the rest, taken from real training orders, with the purchase month set explicitly
build_scenario <- function(label, seller, cust, month) {
  rows <- train |> filter(seller_state == seller, customer_state == cust)
  stopifnot(nrow(rows) > 0)

  rows |>
    summarise(
      across(where(is.numeric), \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      across(where(is.factor), mode_level)
    ) |>
    select(-delivery_days) |>
    mutate(
      order_id = "scenario",
      purchase_month = factor(as.character(month), levels = levels(train$purchase_month)),
      label = label,
      n_similar = nrow(rows),
      route_median_days = median(rows$delivery_days)
    )
}

scenario_def <- tribble(
  ~label,                                   ~seller, ~cust, ~month,
  "Same state (SP to SP), off-peak (Aug)",  "SP",    "SP",  8,
  "Same state (SP to SP), peak (Nov)",      "SP",    "SP",  11,
  "Neighbouring state (SP to RJ), Aug",     "SP",    "RJ",  8,
  "Northeast (SP to BA), off-peak (Aug)",   "SP",    "BA",  8,
  "Northeast (SP to BA), peak (Nov)",       "SP",    "BA",  11,
  "Remote north (SP to AM), off-peak (Aug)", "SP",   "AM",  8
)

scn_df <- pmap(scenario_def, build_scenario) |> list_rbind()

scn_res <- scn_df |>
  mutate(
    lasso_pred = predict(fit_lasso3, new_data = scn_df)$.pred,
    tree_pred  = predict(fit_tree3,  new_data = scn_df)$.pred,
    olist_estimate = estimated_days
  ) |>
  select(label, n_similar, route_median_days, olist_estimate, lasso_pred, tree_pred)

scn_res |>
  transmute(
    Scenario = label,
    `Similar training orders` = format(n_similar, big.mark = ","),
    `Route median, all months (days)` = round(route_median_days, 1),
    `Olist estimate (days)` = round(olist_estimate, 1),
    `Lasso prediction (days)` = round(lasso_pred, 1),
    `Tree prediction (days)` = round(tree_pred, 1)
  ) |>
  kable(caption = "Predicted delivery days for six typical order profiles")
```

```{r}
#| label: scenario-plot
#| fig-cap: "Model prediction (bars) vs. Olist's checkout estimate (diamonds) for six order profiles"
#| fig-height: 4.5
scn_res |>
  mutate(label = fct_reorder(label, tree_pred)) |>
  ggplot(aes(y = label)) +
  geom_col(aes(x = tree_pred), fill = "#2b8cbe", width = 0.6) +
  geom_point(aes(x = olist_estimate), shape = 18, size = 4, color = "#d95f02") +
  labs(
    title = "Same seller, different routes: predicted delivery time",
    subtitle = "Bars: decision tree prediction. Diamonds: Olist's estimate for the same profile",
    x = "Days", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: scenario-values
#| include: false
lo_row <- scn_res[which.min(scn_res$tree_pred), ]
hi_row <- scn_res[which.max(scn_res$tree_pred), ]
same_off  <- scn_res$tree_pred[1]
same_peak <- scn_res$tree_pred[2]
ne_off    <- scn_res$tree_pred[4]
ne_peak   <- scn_res$tree_pred[5]
lasso_same_off  <- scn_res$lasso_pred[1]
lasso_same_peak <- scn_res$lasso_pred[2]
lasso_ne_off    <- scn_res$lasso_pred[4]
lasso_ne_peak   <- scn_res$lasso_pred[5]
max_model_gap <- max(abs(scn_res$lasso_pred - scn_res$tree_pred))
olist_gap <- scn_res$olist_estimate - scn_res$tree_pred
```

**What the scenarios show**

- **Route changes the answer more than anything else.** Predicted delivery runs from `r round(lo_row$tree_pred, 1)` days (`r lo_row$label`) to `r round(hi_row$tree_pred, 1)` days (`r hi_row$label`) according to the tree.
- **The peak month adds days on the same route.** Moving the same-state order from August to November changes the tree prediction by `r sprintf("%+.1f", same_peak - same_off)` days (lasso: `r sprintf("%+.1f", lasso_same_peak - lasso_same_off)`), and moving the Bahia order by `r sprintf("%+.1f", ne_peak - ne_off)` days (lasso: `r sprintf("%+.1f", lasso_ne_peak - lasso_ne_off)`). The size of the seasonal effect depends on the route, which only the tree can express fully.
- **The two models agree on the direction, not always on the size.** They differ by up to `r round(max_model_gap, 1)` days across the six profiles. Where they disagree most, treat the prediction as less certain. The remote-north profile also rests on few similar orders, so read it as an illustration only.
- **Olist's estimate also changes with route, but not in step with the model.** The estimate minus the tree prediction ranges from `r round(min(olist_gap), 1)` to `r round(max(olist_gap), 1)` days across the six profiles, so the amount of padding is not the same for every route.

These profiles use real typical values for each route, and the purchase year is set to the most common year on that route. They illustrate the model; they are not forecasts of any single order.

---

## Late deliveries by purchase month

```{r}
#| label: monthly
month_tbl <- tp |>
  mutate(month_num = as.integer(as.character(purchase_month))) |>
  group_by(month_num) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    actual = mean(delivery_days),
    olist = mean(estimated_days),
    late = mean(delivery_days > estimated_days),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(month = factor(month.abb[month_num], levels = month.abb))

ggplot(month_tbl, aes(x = month, y = late)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2b8cbe", width = 0.7) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Share of orders arriving after Olist's estimate, by purchase month",
    subtitle = "Test set, all years pooled",
    x = NULL, y = "Late vs. estimate"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

```{r}
#| label: monthly-values
#| include: false
late_top <- month_tbl |> arrange(desc(late)) |> slice_head(n = 3)
late_low <- month_tbl |> arrange(late) |> slice_head(n = 1)
slow_month_note <- "Compare this with the average delivery time by purchase month in the Exploration page (Section 4.5)."
```

The late share is highest for orders placed in `r paste(as.character(late_top$month), collapse = ", ")` (`r paste(scales::percent(late_top$late, accuracy = 0.1), collapse = ", ")`) and lowest in `r as.character(late_low$month)` (`r scales::percent(late_low$late, accuracy = 0.1)`). Months pool different years in a dataset that covers 2016 to 2018, so some of this reflects specific events or demand peaks in a single year, not a calendar pattern. `r slow_month_note`

---

## What the team should do

1. **Make the delivery promise route-aware.** Set the checkout estimate from seller state, customer state, and month, instead of one rule for everything. The tier table shows how unevenly the current estimate is padded (`r round(pad_lo, 1)` days on `r pad_lo_tier`, `r round(pad_hi, 1)` days on `r pad_hi_tier`). Same-state routes are the natural first pilot: they are the most predictable tier (average miss of `r round(same_tier$mae, 1)` days) and today's estimate there is `r round(same_tier$olist, 1)` days against `r round(same_tier$actual, 1)` actual. The buffer should be chosen so the late rate stays at or below today's `r scales::percent(same_tier$olist_late, accuracy = 0.1)` on that tier. A pilot on a few routes would show how many days could be saved. *Measure it by:* average promised days and the late rate, by route tier.

2. **Show a delivery window, not a single date.** Point predictions are good on average but miss the slow tail, and the width of the uncertainty depends on the route (about `r round(narrow_width)` days on the tightest tier and `r round(wide_width)` days on `r wide_tier`, measured as the middle 80% of outcomes). Offering "between day X and day Y" is more honest and matches how the model behaves. *Measure it by:* the share of orders that land inside the window, which should be close to the 80% it is designed for.

3. **Add a seasonal buffer for the slow months.** Orders placed in `r paste(as.character(late_top$month), collapse = ", ")` are late most often. Extend the promise or add carrier capacity in those months. Check whether the pattern holds in newer data before committing. *Measure it by:* the late rate in those months, year over year.

4. **Treat the north and northeast as a separate service tier.** Routes into these regions are the slowest and the hardest to predict (the highest-error tier is `r mae_hi_tier`, with an average miss of `r round(mae_hi, 1)` days). Set separate expectations, review carrier performance on these lanes, and consider whether stocking inventory closer to these customers is worth testing. *Measure it by:* delivery time and prediction error on these lanes, tracked separately.

5. **Test whether sourcing closer to the buyer helps.** Same-state routes are the fastest, and the same-state flag is among the most important features in the tree (second only to customer state). That is an association, not proof that moving a seller would change delivery time, because sellers and buyers in the same state may also differ in carrier mix and product type. A small pilot, such as a "ships from your state" badge or search ranking, would show whether the effect is real. *Measure it by:* conversion and delivery time on the pilot group against a control.

6. **Do not spend effort on purchase weekday or time of day.** In the Exploration page, weekday moved average delivery time by under two days and time of day by well under a day, against a gap of about a week between same-state and cross-state routes. Put effort into route, carrier, and seller handling instead.

7. **Look at seller handling time.** The shipping deadline the seller was given (`ship_window_days`) is a predictor in the models, and the Exploration page shows median delivery time differing across shipping-window groups. We cannot tell from this data whether sellers who are given more time actually take more time, so this is a question to investigate with seller-level shipping timestamps.

8. **Keep the model honest over time.** Retrain on recent orders at a regular interval, watch average error by route tier, and treat a sustained rise in error as a sign that carrier performance or demand has shifted.

---

## How far to trust it

- **Accuracy is useful, not exact.** A typical miss is about `r round(best_row$mae, 1)` days, and the average error is much smaller than the error on the worst orders (RMSE `r round(best_row$rmse, 1)` days). This is good for checkout windows and capacity planning, not for day-exact commitments.
- **The slow tail is still hard.** The model under-predicts the slowest orders, because it predicts a typical value for a right-skewed target. That is why we recommend a window with a buffer.
- **A random split tests similar orders, not future ones.** The test orders come from the same 2016 to 2018 period as the training orders. The model has not been tested on a new carrier contract, a strike, or a different year.
- **Single test set.** Differences of a few hundredths of a day between models are not meaningful.
- **Order-item grain.** `delivery_days` is an order-level duration repeated across the items of an order, so multi-item orders carry slightly more weight in the metrics.
- **Associations, not causes.** The importance scores and coefficients show what the models rely on to predict. They do not show what causes a delay, which is why recommendations 5 and 7 are framed as tests.
- **Coarse geography.** Zip-code region is only a rough stand-in for distance, and the scenarios use median values for each route.

## What would improve it next

- **Real seller-to-customer distance** from Olist's geolocation table, which is the most promising feature not yet used.
- **Stage-level timestamps** (approval, handoff to carrier, delivery), so seller handling time and carrier transit time can be modelled separately and each team can see its own share.
- **A time-based test**: train on earlier months and test on later ones, which is a stricter check than a random split.
- **Non-linear ensemble models and a log-transformed target.** These were outside the scope here and were not tested on the order-grouped split. They might lower typical error, at the cost of being harder to explain.
